title: Table tennis glossary: from banana flick to chiquita
seo_title: Table tennis glossary: terms explained from A to Z
description: A plain-English table tennis glossary: the shots, spins, rules, kit and competition terms you will hear at a club or on a stream, each briefly explained.
summary: The words you will hear at your club or on a WTT stream, from banana flick to the expedite rule, each explained in a sentence or two, with links to the full guides.
key_points: Strokes: loop, push, chop, block, flick and smash cover most shots you will see.
Spin words: topspin, backspin, sidespin and float describe how the ball rotates.
Rules words: let, deuce, game, match and expedite come from the ITTF Laws.
Kit words: blade, rubber, sponge, pimples and anti-spin describe the bat.
body: Table tennis has its own vocabulary, and commentators and coaches use it freely. This glossary explains the terms you are most likely to hear, grouped alphabetically. Where a term comes from the rules, the definition follows the ITTF Laws; where it has a full guide, we link to it.
## A to B
**All-rounder**: A player equally happy attacking and defending. See [playing styles](/guide/table-tennis-playing-styles.html).
**Anti-spin**: A smooth rubber with very little grip, so it is barely affected by the opponent's spin. A specialist defensive choice.

**Backspin**: Spin where the bottom of the ball rotates forwards. It makes the ball float and drop into the net off an unprepared bat. Also called underspin. See [spin explained](/guide/spin-in-table-tennis-explained.html).

**Banana flick**: A backhand flick played with sidespin and topspin, named after the curved path of the bat. The ITTF credits Petr Korbel with its first use; it spread from China from the late 2000s. Also called the chiquita.
**Blade**: The wooden part of the bat, before any rubber goes on. See [blades explained](/guide/table-tennis-blades-explained.html).
**Block**: A short stroke played just after the bounce that uses the opponent's pace to send the ball back.
## C to F
**Chiquita**: Another name for the banana flick.
**Chop**: A defensive stroke played from well back, cutting down on the ball to give heavy backspin. Players who rely on it are choppers; Eleven's site [The Chop](/defensive/) follows them.
**Counterloop**: A loop played against the opponent's loop, usually from away from the table.
**Crossover**: The point, usually near the elbow, where a player switches between forehand and backhand. A favourite target.
**Deuce**: The score of 10-10. From then on a game is won by the first player to lead by two points, and each player serves one point in turn.

**Expedite rule**: The rule that speeds up long games. If a game lasts 10 minutes, unless 18 points have been scored, players serve one point each in turn and the receiver wins the point by making 13 good returns.
**Flick**: An attacking stroke against a short ball over the table, played mainly with the wrist and forearm. Called a flip in the US.
**Float**: A serve or push with little or no spin, made to look as if it has plenty.
## G to L
**Game**: The first player to 11 points wins a game, unless it reaches 10-10 (see deuce). See [scoring explained](/guide/table-tennis-scoring-explained.html).
**Inverted rubber**: Rubber with its pimples facing inwards, giving a smooth surface that grips the ball. What most players use on both sides.
**LARC**: The ITTF's list of authorised racket coverings, the rubbers approved for competition.
**Let**: A rally that is not scored and is replayed, most often when a serve touches the net and lands correctly.
**Lob**: A high defensive return from far back, played against smashes.
**Long pimples**: Rubber with tall, thin pimples that bend on contact and return the ball with unpredictable spin.
**Loop**: A heavy topspin stroke that brushes up the back of the ball; the basic attacking stroke of the modern game.
## M to P
**Match**: The best of an odd number of games, usually five or seven.
**Multiball**: Training in which a coach feeds balls quickly one after another from a box, rather than playing rallies.
**Obstruction**: Touching the ball before it has bounced on your side while it is above or travelling towards the table. You lose the point.
**Penhold**: Holding the bat like a pen, between thumb and forefinger. See [penhold and shakehand](/guide/penhold-vs-shakehand-grip.html).
**Pimples, or pips**: Rubber played with the pimples facing out. Short pimples blunt the opponent's spin; long pimples reverse and disguise it.
**Push**: A short backspin stroke against backspin, played over the table to keep the ball low.
## R to S
**Racket**: The official word for the bat.
**Rally**: The period during which the ball is in play, from the toss of the serve to the point or let.
**Reverse penhold backhand**: A penhold backhand played with the back of the bat, which lets penholders attack on that side.
**Rubber**: The covering on each side of the blade. In team competitions, an individual match within a tie is also called a rubber.
**Shakehand**: The common grip, holding the handle as if shaking hands.
**Sidespin**: Spin around a vertical axis, which makes the ball curve and kick sideways.
**Smash**: A flat, fast hit to finish the point, usually against a high ball.
**Speed glue**: Solvent-based glue once brushed on to rubbers for extra speed. Banned since 2008.

**Sponge**: The layer under the top sheet of an inverted rubber. Its thickness and hardness change speed and control. See [sponge thickness and hardness](/guide/rubber-sponge-thickness-hardness.html).
**Strawberry flick**: A backhand flick with the opposite sidespin to the banana flick.
## T to Z
**Third ball**: The server's first shot after the return of serve, often the first attack. See [serve and receive tactics](/guide/serve-and-receive-tactics.html).
**Tie**: A team match made up of several individual matches. See [how team matches work](/guide/team-table-tennis-format.html).
**Topspin**: Spin where the top of the ball rotates forwards. It makes the ball dip on to the table and jump off the opponent's bat.

Once the words make sense, the next step is to see them in action: [rules explained](/guide/table-tennis-rules-explained.html) puts the basics together, and the [events page](/events/) shows what is on to watch.
